Have you ever heard that learning a language can slow down ageing? It sounds almost too good to be true, so let's look at what the research actually says.

In 2025, a large study was published in the journal Nature Aging. Researchers looked at more than eighty-six thousand people, aged fifty-one to ninety, in twenty-seven European countries. People who spoke only one language were more likely to be ageing faster than expected. And the more languages people spoke, the lower that risk was.

There's an important catch, though. A study like this shows a link, not a cause. People who speak several languages may be different in other ways, too.

So is it worth starting later in life? A study in Scotland found that people who learned a second language as adults also did better in old age than their childhood test scores predicted. But in a Swedish trial, older adults who took an eleven-week Italian course showed no change in their memory.

The honest answer is that we don't know for sure yet. But a new language gives you a reason to talk to new people. And that can't hurt.

Hey, everyone, and welcome back to Small Wins, the show about the tiny things that quietly change your life. I'm your host, and I'm so glad you're here.

Grab a coffee and put your feet up, because today's episode is a good one. We're talking about the five-minute rule. Here's the idea. When you don't feel like doing something, you tell yourself, I'll just do it for five minutes. That's it. Five minutes, and then I can stop.

And here's the funny thing. You almost never stop. Because the hardest part was never the work. It was starting.

I tried this last month with running. I hate running. I really do. But every morning I said, five minutes, just around the block. And guess what? This morning I ran for half an hour, and I didn't even notice.

So today, I've got a guest who used this little trick to write an entire book. But first, a quick question for you. What's the one thing you keep putting off? Hold that thought, because by the end of this episode, you're going to start it.

Let's get into it.

All right, everyone, come a little closer. Don't be shy, there's room at the front.

Most people are surprised by how small she is. And some of you are probably wondering, why this one? Why does the whole world come to see this painting, when there are bigger, brighter, more dramatic ones just down the hall?

Here's the secret. For four hundred years, she was famous in the art world, and almost nowhere else. Then, on a quiet Monday morning in August of nineteen eleven, while the museum was closed, a man who had once worked here lifted her off the wall and walked out with the painting hidden under his work clothes.

How long do you think it took before anyone noticed she was gone? A full day.

And that is when everything changed. Newspapers around the world printed her face on the front page, so people who had never set foot in a museum suddenly knew exactly what she looked like. The police even questioned a young Pablo Picasso. And here, in this museum, crowds lined up just to stare at the empty space on the wall.

For more than two years, the whole world wondered where she was. So when she was finally found in Florence and brought back to Paris, she was no longer just a painting. She was the most famous face on earth.

So take one more look at that smile, and tell me: if no one had ever stolen her, would you be standing here today?

Good morning, everyone, and happy Friday. Let's take a look at the weekend, because I have some good news, and I'm going to make you wait for it.

First, the not-so-good part. That band of rain that's been sitting over us all week isn't done yet. This morning we're looking at heavy showers in the north and along the coast, with gusts of up to forty miles an hour by lunchtime. If you're driving to work, give yourself a few extra minutes, and please, take the big umbrella, not the cute one.

This afternoon, temperatures will struggle to get past nine degrees, and tonight they'll drop to around two, so if you have plants on the balcony, bring them inside.

Now, here's the part you've been waiting for. Late tomorrow morning, a high pressure system moves in from the west and pushes all of this out to sea. By Saturday afternoon, we're expecting clear blue skies, light winds, and highs of fifteen degrees. Sunday looks even better.

That's right. After three gray weeks, the sun is finally coming back.

So, here's my question for you. What are you going to do with the first sunny weekend in almost a month?

Your heart is racing, your hands are cold, and you're about to speak in front of people. Most of us tell ourselves the same thing: calm down. But what if that's the wrong advice?

In 2014, Alison Wood Brooks, a researcher at Harvard Business School, put it to the test. She asked people to give a short speech in front of a camera. Right before they started, some said out loud, "I am calm." Others said, "I am excited."

Then other people watched the videos and rated them. The speakers who had said "I am excited" came across as more confident and more persuasive.

Why would one sentence make a difference? Being nervous and being excited feel almost the same in the body. Either way, your heart beats faster. Calming down is hard, but giving the same feeling a different name is easy.

There's a catch, though. The nerves didn't go away. People still felt anxious. And later studies haven't always found the same effect, so this isn't a magic trick.

But it costs nothing to try. Before you press record, say it once: I'm excited.

Hey everyone, welcome back. So, last night I rewatched Interstellar, for maybe the tenth time, and I need to talk about it, because it hit me harder than ever. No spoilers for the ending, I promise.

Quick setup. Earth is dying. Dust storms everywhere, crops failing, and a former pilot named Cooper leaves his kids behind to fly through a wormhole and find humanity a new home.

Now, what makes this movie special? First, the science is real. Christopher Nolan worked with the physicist Kip Thorne, and the black hole you see on screen was built from his equations. It looked so real that it ended up in scientific papers.

Second, the music. Hans Zimmer used a huge church organ, and when it kicks in during the docking scene, I swear, I forgot to breathe.

But here's the scene that gets me every single time. They land on a planet where one hour equals seven years back on Earth. When Cooper gets back to the ship, twenty-three years of messages from his kids are waiting for him. He watches them grow up in a few minutes, and he can't say a word back.

Is it perfect? No. Some of the dialogue is a bit heavy, and it's almost three hours long. But I've never seen a movie make physics feel this personal.

So here's my question for you. If you could send one message to someone across time, who would it be, and what would you say?
